groups.high: The Sphere Handbook 2018 uses 15 litres per person per day as an established minimum planning quantity for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene in humanitarian emergencies. For a family of four, that planning quantity is 60 litres per day before adjustment for context. Context matters: climate, health, cultural practices and the stage of the response can require more water or a different initial provision. This is not a universal ceiling or a guarantee that every sanitation system can operate on that quantity. Water should be safe and available equitably, including to people with disabilities. Water points should be within 500 metres of households, and queuing should take no more than 30 minutes. These are separate access indicators, not a prescribed walking-speed calculation. Assess the safety of the route, the effort of carrying water and barriers affecting children, older people and other vulnerable groups. Monitor actual quantities collected, water quality and access, rather than simply counting installed taps. If provision falls short, explain the constraints to the community and work towards adequate, safe access.
groups.mid: In emergencies, safe water is needed for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene. The Sphere Handbook 2018 uses 15 litres per person per day as a minimum planning amount. A family of four would need about 60 litres at that level. Local conditions can change this amount. Heat, illness and people's usual needs all matter. So does the stage of the response. The initial provision may differ from what can be supplied later. This is not a cap on aid. It may not cover toilets that use water. Water points should be within 500 metres of homes. Waits should be no more than 30 minutes. Distance and waiting time are separate checks, not a rule based on walking speed. Teams should also check that paths are safe. Can everyone collect water? Older people, children and people with disabilities may need extra help. They may struggle to reach the source or carry containers. Check water quality as well as the amount people actually take home. Counting installed taps alone does not show adequate access. Identify households that are excluded and work to remove barriers. When supplies fall short, explain the problem and work towards safe, adequate access.
groups.low: In an emergency, people need safe water to drink, cook and wash. The Sphere Handbook 2018 uses 15 litres for each person each day as a minimum planning amount. A family of four would need about 60 litres a day at that level. Some people need more. Heat, illness and local needs can change the amount. So can the stage of the response. The initial supply may differ from what can be given later. It is not a limit on how much aid teams may give. It may not meet all the needs of toilets that use water. Water points should be within 500 metres of homes. The wait in line should be no more than 30 minutes. These are two separate checks. They are not a rule worked out from walking speed. Teams should also check whether the path is safe. Think about people who cannot walk far or carry heavy cans. Children, older people and people with disabilities may need help. Water must be safe to use, not just close by. Aid teams should check how much people really collect and who is left out. Counting installed taps alone does not show enough access. If supply falls short, teams should explain why and work to improve it.
groups.source_review: Checked Sphere quantity, distance and queuing indicators; context-qualified planning guidance.
groups.notes: Removed invented 2.5 km/h derivation and categorical claim that 15 litres covers flushing toilets. Root claim-level review aligned the shared family-of-four arithmetic example, response-stage caveat, vulnerable groups and access monitoring across levels.

groups.high: Impartial assistance means allocating humanitarian relief according to assessed need, with priority for the most urgent distress. The Red Cross and Red Crescent principles and the disaster-relief Code of Conduct reject discrimination based on nationality, race, religious belief, class or political opinion. Food, medical care, shelter and protection should not depend on whether recipients support a government, armed group or donor. Equal respect does not require identical allocations: a person facing greater danger or more severe deprivation may need more support. Agencies should assess needs fairly and explain selection criteria so that neglected groups can challenge exclusion. Impartiality is distinct from neutrality. Impartiality governs who receives help; neutrality concerns not taking sides in hostilities or political disputes. Both can support trust and humanitarian access, but neither guarantees that workers will be safe or admitted to every conflict area.
groups.mid: Impartial assistance means aid is based on need. The most urgent cases come first. The Red Cross and Red Crescent principles and the disaster-relief Code of Conduct set out this approach. Do not choose people by nationality, race, faith, class or political opinion. Medical care, food, shelter and protection should never depend on support for a government, armed group or donor. Fair treatment need not mean equal shares. Greater danger or need may call for more help. Agencies should assess needs openly and explain their selection criteria. People who are excluded need a way to question the decision and raise concerns. Impartiality differs from neutrality. Both matter in aid work. Impartiality means help by need. Neutrality means not taking sides in war or political disputes. These principles can build trust and improve access to people in conflict. They do not guarantee safe passage or entry to every area. Aid groups still need to manage safety risks.
groups.low: Aid should go to people because they need it. Those in the greatest danger should get help first. This means fair aid based on need. The Red Cross and Red Crescent principles and the disaster-relief Code of Conduct set out this rule. A person's race, faith, class, nationality or political views must not decide whether they get help. Food, health care, shelter and protection must not be rewards for supporting a government or armed group. Fair aid does not always mean equal shares. A person with more urgent needs may need more support. Aid teams should check needs and explain who can get help. People who are left out should be able to raise concerns. Fair aid and not taking sides are not the same. The first means help is based on need. The second means not taking sides in a conflict or political dispute. Both can build trust. Neither can promise that aid workers will always be safe or allowed in.
groups.source_review: Checked impartiality, neutrality and Code of Conduct principles.
groups.notes: Corrected conflation of impartiality with neutrality and removed guaranteed operational access.

groups.high: UN Secretary-General's Bulletin ST/SGB/2003/13 prohibits sexual exploitation and sexual abuse by UN staff. Exploitation includes abusing vulnerability, unequal power or trust for sexual purposes. Abuse includes actual or threatened sexual intrusion by force or under unequal or coercive conditions. Exchanging money, employment, goods, services or assistance for sex is prohibited. Sexual activity with anyone under 18 is prohibited regardless of the local age of consent; mistaken belief about age is not a defence. The bulletin contains a limited pre-existing lawful-marriage provision, not a general local-law exception. Sexual relationships with beneficiaries are strongly discouraged because of unequal power. Staff must report concerns through established channels; managers must maintain an environment that prevents abuse. Serious misconduct can lead to disciplinary measures, including summary dismissal. Referral for criminal action depends on the circumstances and applicable law. Partner arrangements must address these standards. Zero tolerance means allegations require appropriate action and fair procedures, not automatic guilt or a guarantee of criminal conviction.
groups.mid: UN Bulletin ST/SGB/2003/13 bans sexual exploitation and abuse by UN staff. No worker may use a person's need, trust or lack of power to get sex. Abuse includes forced or threatened sexual acts. It also includes acts under unfair power or pressure. Workers must not trade aid, money, jobs, goods or services for sex. Sex with anyone under 18 is banned, even if local law sets a lower age. Getting the age wrong is not a defence. The text has a narrow rule for a lawful marriage that already existed. That is not a broad exception based on local law. Sexual relationships with people who receive aid are strongly discouraged. The worker has more power. Staff must report concerns through the proper channels. Managers must act to prevent abuse. Serious misconduct can lead to dismissal. Criminal action depends on the case and the law. Partner agreements must address these rules too. Zero tolerance means taking concerns seriously and using fair checks. It does not mean guilt without a fair process.
groups.low: UN Bulletin ST/SGB/2003/13 bans sexual exploitation and abuse by UN staff. No worker may use a person's need, trust or lack of power to get sex. Abuse includes forced or threatened sexual acts. It also includes acts under unfair power or pressure. Workers must not trade aid, money, jobs, goods or services for sex. Sex with anyone under 18 is banned, even if local law sets a lower age. Getting the age wrong is not a defence. The text has a narrow rule for a lawful marriage that already existed. That is not a broad exception based on local law. Sexual relationships with people who receive aid are strongly discouraged. The worker has more power. Staff must report concerns through the proper channels. Managers must act to prevent abuse. Serious misconduct can lead to dismissal. Court action depends on the case and the law. Partner agreements must address these rules too. Zero tolerance means taking concerns seriously and using fair checks. It does not mean guilt without a fair process.
groups.source_review: Checked bulletin definitions, prohibitions, reporting, managerial duties and partner provisions. Included section 4.4 marriage qualification.
groups.notes: Removed claims bulletin mandates independent investigations, universal contractor scope and automatic prosecution. Corrected abuse definition and added specific child/sex-for-aid rules.

groups.high: The Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability, revised in 2024, requires meaningful information-sharing with people affected by crises. People should understand the assistance available, who is eligible, how selection works and how to obtain support. Agencies should explain their role, what they can realistically provide and any relevant limits or changes. Information must be timely, accurate and accessible in languages and formats people can use. Written notices alone may exclude people with low literacy or disabilities. Meetings, audio, accessible formats and trusted local channels may also be needed. People should know how to ask questions, give feedback and make safe complaints, including about unfair exclusion. Where an appeal or review procedure exists, explain it clearly. Communicating with communities should be two-way: listen, answer questions and use feedback to improve decisions. The CHS is a humanitarian accountability standard, not a universal statute guaranteeing unrestricted access to every agency's budget or confidential records.
groups.mid: The Core Humanitarian Standard, or CHS, was revised in 2024. It says people in a crisis should get clear facts about aid. Say what help is on offer and who can get it. Explain how people are chosen and how they can ask for help. Be clear about limits, delays and changes in plans. Share news in time for people to act, using the words and language they know. A written notice will not work for all. Some people need speech, sound or other forms they can use because of low literacy or disability. People should know where to ask questions and how to make a safe complaint. Explain any way to seek a review of a decision. Listen to people as well as giving them facts, and use their views to improve aid. The CHS is a standard for accountable aid work. It is not a law that gives everyone access to all private files and budgets.
groups.low: People have a right to know about aid that affects them. The Core Humanitarian Standard, or CHS, was revised in 2024. It says aid teams should share clear facts with people in a crisis. Say what help is on offer. Say who can get it and how people are chosen. Explain how to ask for help. Be clear about limits and changes. Use the words and language people know. Share news in time for people to act. A written notice will not work for all. Some people need speech, sound or other forms they can use. People should know how to ask questions. They should know how to give views or make a safe complaint. Explain any way to seek a review of a decision. Listen to people as well as giving them facts. Use what they say to improve the aid. CHS is a standard for good aid work. It is not a law that opens all private files or budgets to everyone.
groups.source_review: Checked CHS 2024 communication, participation and complaints requirements.
groups.notes: Removed unsupported universal budget disclosure and statutory-entitlement claims.

groups.high: Participation under the Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability means that people affected by crises can influence the actions and decisions that concern them. Agencies should involve communities in assessing needs, designing assistance, monitoring results and improving programmes. Include women, young people, people with disabilities and groups whose views are often excluded. Participation must be safe and accessible, with suitable languages, meeting times and ways to contribute. A meeting with a few powerful leaders is not sufficient evidence that everyone's views were heard. Explain what decisions communities can influence, the constraints on the programme and how their input affected the outcome. Provide continuing feedback and complaints channels. Support people's skills and local organisations rather than displacing them. The CHS does not prescribe a universal 40% membership quota or require 20–30% of every project budget to be spent on participation. Meaningful influence, inclusion and accountability matter more than invented numerical targets or consultation without follow-through.
groups.mid: People affected by crises should help shape the aid they receive. The Core Humanitarian Standard, or CHS, calls for a real say in decisions. A meeting after plans are fixed is not enough. Ask communities about their needs. Include them in project design, checks and changes. Include women, young people, people with disabilities and others whose views are often missed. A few powerful local leaders cannot represent every household or concern. Use languages people know and methods they can use. Choose times that allow different groups to take part safely. Explain which choices people can affect. Say which limits cannot change. Then tell them how their views affected the outcome. Keep feedback and complaints channels open throughout the project. Support local skills and organisations rather than replacing them. CHS means Core Humanitarian Standard, not Community Health System. It sets no fixed 40% quota for women and youth. It does not require a 20–30% budget share for taking part. A real say and fair access matter more than invented targets.
groups.low: People affected by crises should help shape the assistance they receive. The Core Humanitarian Standard, or CHS, calls for their views to affect plans and choices. Assess community needs before an assistance programme starts. Involve them in the design, checks and changes. Include women, young people and people with disabilities. Reach those who are often left out. A meeting with a few local leaders may miss many views. Make it safe to speak. Use languages people know and times they can attend. Offer other ways to give views if a meeting is not safe or practical. Say which choices people can affect and what limits there are. Then explain how their views changed the plan. Keep accessible feedback and complaints channels open throughout the programme. Help local groups build skills rather than replacing them. CHS means Core Humanitarian Standard, not Community Health System. It does not set a 40% quota for women and youth. It does not set a 20–30% budget share for taking part. Do not treat those numbers as CHS rules.
groups.source_review: Checked CHS participation and inclusion; numerical claims absent from standard.
groups.notes: Corrected expansion of CHS, removed invented Social Capital Hypothesis foundation, veto right, quotas and budget mandates. Final claim-level spot review retained this practical qualification explicitly in Low.

groups.high: Safe programming requires humanitarian agencies to prevent and reduce harm linked to their activities. Under the Core Humanitarian Standard, assistance should protect people's safety, dignity and rights rather than increase their exposure to violence, exploitation or exclusion. Assess the context before choosing distribution sites, routes, eligibility rules or data practices. A poorly located water point may expose people to attack; public beneficiary lists may reveal sensitive information; unfair selection may intensify local tensions. These are risks to investigate, not inevitable outcomes of aid. Involve affected people, including groups facing particular barriers, in identifying dangers and designing safer options. Avoid assuming that established leaders represent everyone. Monitor risks throughout delivery because conditions change. Provide safe feedback and complaints channels, train staff and adjust, suspend or redesign activities when serious harm cannot be adequately controlled. Record decisions and communicate changes. Safe programming is an ongoing duty to manage foreseeable risks, not a promise that every emergency operation will be risk-free.
groups.mid: The Core Humanitarian Standard says aid should protect people's safety, dignity and rights. Safe programming means checking that aid does not cause avoidable harm. Assess the place, routes, selection rules and data practices before work begins. An unsafe path to a water point may expose people to attack. A public list of names may reveal private details. Unfair selection may increase tensions within a community. These are possible risks to check. They are not outcomes that always follow aid. Ask local people how they could be affected. What safer options would work? Include those who face barriers. Do not rely only on leaders. Train staff and offer safe ways to raise concerns. Keep reviewing risks. Conditions may change during delivery. Adjust the plan when needed. Pause and redesign work if serious harm cannot be controlled. Explain changes and record the reasons for decisions. Safe programming means managing foreseeable harm. It cannot promise no risk.
groups.low: Aid should help people without putting them in more danger. The Core Humanitarian Standard calls for this safe approach. Check risks before aid starts. Look at the place, routes, rules and use of personal data. A water point on an unsafe path may expose people to attack. A public list of names may reveal private facts. Unfair rules may raise tensions in the community. These risks do not happen in every project. Teams must check the local facts. Ask people what feels unsafe and what could help. Include those who find it hard to speak or reach services. Do not rely only on local leaders. Keep checking as the work goes on. Risks can change. Train staff and give people a safe way to raise concerns. Change the plan when needed. If serious harm cannot be controlled, pause or redesign the work. Explain changes and keep a record of decisions. Safe aid means working to reduce harm. It cannot mean a promise of no risk at all.
groups.source_review: Checked CHS do-no-harm and safeguarding obligations; examples framed as risks rather than universal facts.
groups.notes: Replaced vague strategic claims with assess-design-monitor-adapt actions and feedback safeguards.

groups.high: Personal data protection is part of protecting people affected by conflict and other crises. The ICRC Rules on Personal Data Protection, revised in 2020, require a legitimate basis, specified purposes, proportionate collection and appropriate security. Collect only what is necessary and explain why information is needed, how it may be shared and how concerns can be raised. Purpose limitation does not mean that every compatible humanitarian use or justified archival purpose is forbidden. Retention should be reviewed; data no longer needed should be erased or otherwise handled under a justified retention or archival basis. Protect information through measures appropriate to the risks, including encryption where appropriate, access controls, secure transfer, key management and staff training. Encryption alone does not prevent misuse by an authorised user. Avoid publishing sensitive identities or locations. Mishandling can expose people to violence, stigma or exploitation. The rules do not establish a universal AES-256 requirement, nor did the reviewed source confirm the claimed 2025 revision. Apply the actual rules and risk assessment rather than treating a particular algorithm as a complete ethical policy.
groups.mid: Personal data can expose people in a crisis to violence, stigma or exploitation. The ICRC Rules on Personal Data Protection were revised in 2020. They require a valid basis and clear purpose for using data. Collect only needed details. Explain why they are needed and who may receive them. Say how concerns can be raised. Do not use data for an unrelated purpose without a proper basis. Some linked humanitarian uses may be allowed. Some archive uses may be justified too. Purpose limitation is not a ban on every later use. Review retention periods and delete data when there is no valid reason to keep it. Protect data that is stored or sent. Control access and train staff. Use encryption where appropriate. Encryption scrambles data, but its keys also need protection. It cannot prevent every misuse by someone who already has access. Avoid publishing sensitive names or locations. The reviewed rules do not demand AES-256 in every case. A claimed 2025 revision was not confirmed. Data protection needs a risk-based plan. One algorithm is not enough.
groups.low: A person's data can put them at risk in a crisis. Names, health details or locations may expose them to harm. The ICRC Rules on Personal Data Protection were revised in 2020. They require a valid basis and a clear purpose for using data. Collect only what is needed. Explain why you need it and who may receive it. Tell people how to raise a concern. Do not use the data for an unrelated aim without a proper basis. Some linked aid uses or justified archive uses may be allowed. Check how long data is needed. Delete it or use a valid rule for keeping it. Protect stored data and data being sent. Use encryption where the risks call for it. This scrambles data so others cannot easily read it. Control access, protect keys and train staff too. Encryption cannot stop every misuse by someone with access. Do not publish sensitive names or locations. The reviewed rules do not require AES-256 in every case. A claimed 2025 revision was not confirmed. Security needs a full plan, not just one type of code.
groups.source_review: Checked official framework and rules on purpose limitation, minimisation, retention, archiving and security.
groups.notes: Corrected absolute service-only retention claim and universal AES-256 mandate; did not assert unverified 2025 revision.

groups.high: Strengthening local capacity means supporting the knowledge, skills, resources and institutions that communities use to manage their own needs. Under the Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability, humanitarian action should recognise and build on local capabilities, leadership and resilience. External agencies should understand existing services and community organisations before creating parallel systems. Involve local actors in defining priorities and decisions, and provide appropriate resources, training and organisational support. Consider who is excluded within local structures: supporting local leadership must not reinforce discrimination or shift unpaid work onto vulnerable people. Agree realistic roles, funding, maintenance and transition arrangements so essential services do not collapse when a project ends. Monitor whether support strengthens rather than displaces local capacity. Avoid unnecessary dependency, but do not withdraw life-saving assistance merely to claim self-reliance; continuing needs and risks matter. CHS means Core Humanitarian Standard, not Capacity for Human Security. It does not impose a universal requirement for private partnerships or financial independence from all future aid.
groups.mid: Local people already have skills, knowledge and ways to help each other. Aid should build on these strengths. This is part of the Core Humanitarian Standard, or CHS. Learn about local services and groups before starting a new system. Let local people help set priorities and make choices. Offer funds, training and other support that meets real needs. Do not assume local leaders speak for everyone. Check whether women, young people or other groups are left out. Do not shift unpaid work onto people who already face hardship. Agree who will run, fund and maintain a service when outside support ends. Check that aid makes local systems stronger rather than replacing them. Avoid creating a need for outside help when it is not needed. But do not stop life-saving aid just to claim that people can cope alone. Needs and risks still matter. CHS means Core Humanitarian Standard. It is not Capacity for Human Security. It does not require all communities to become free of every future form of aid.
groups.low: Local people have skills and knowledge. They have ways to help each other. Aid should build on these strengths. This is part of the Core Humanitarian Standard, or CHS. Learn about local services and groups before starting a new system. Let local people help set priorities and make choices. Offer funds, training and other support that meets real needs. Local leaders may not speak for all. Check whether women, young people or other groups are left out. Do not shift unpaid work onto people who already face hardship. Agree who will run, pay for and maintain the service. Plan this before outside support ends. Check that aid makes local systems stronger rather than replacing them. Avoid creating a need for outside help when it is not needed. But do not stop life-saving aid just to claim that people can cope alone. Needs and risks still matter. CHS means Core Humanitarian Standard. It is not Capacity for Human Security. It does not require all communities to become free of every future form of aid.
groups.source_review: Checked CHS resilience/local capacity, participation and transition principles.
groups.notes: Corrected CHS expansion and removed categorical claims about mandatory market/private-partnership structures. Final claim-level spot review retained this practical qualification explicitly in Low.

groups.high: Resource stewardship means using humanitarian funds responsibly, transparently and in ways that meet affected people's needs. The Grand Bargain includes commitments to publish timely, comparable, open information on humanitarian funding, using the International Aid Transparency Initiative, or IATI, standard. Clear information on commitments, disbursements and activities helps oversight and coordination; publication alone does not establish effectiveness or provide real-time tracing to every individual recipient. The original Grand Bargain also included a target of at least 25% of humanitarian funding reaching local and national responders as directly as possible by 2020. This was a collective policy commitment, not a universally enforceable legal obligation or proof that the target was achieved. Grand Bargain 2.0 began in 2021; a further phase was agreed in 2023. Support for local actors should include fair partnership, suitable funding and accountability without displacing their leadership. Financial transparency must also protect sensitive personal and operational information. Assess the quality and accessibility of data and the actual funding reaching local responders, not just claims of compliance.
groups.mid: Resource stewardship means using aid funds well. Spending should be open to fair checks. The Grand Bargain includes a promise to publish timely facts on aid funds. The IATI standard helps others compare the data. IATI means International Aid Transparency Initiative. Data on promised funds, payments and activities can help teams work together and spot gaps. Publication does not prove success or track every person in real time. The original Grand Bargain set a shared target. At least 25% of aid funds should reach local and national responders as directly as possible by 2020. This is a policy promise, not a law binding everyone. It does not prove the target was met. Grand Bargain 2.0 began in 2021. A further phase was agreed in 2023. Local responders need fair partnerships, appropriate funding and support that respects their leadership. Transparency must protect sensitive personal and operational information. Check the quality and use of published data. Also check the funds local groups really get.
groups.low: Aid money should be used well and be open to fair checks. The Grand Bargain includes a promise to share clear, timely facts about aid funds. The IATI standard helps groups publish these facts in a form others can compare. IATI means International Aid Transparency Initiative. Data on promised funds, payments and work can help people spot gaps or waste. It does not prove every project works. It does not track each person in real time. The original Grand Bargain set a target: at least 25% of aid funds should reach local and national responders as directly as possible by 2020. This was a shared policy promise, not a law binding every agency. A target is not proof it was met. Grand Bargain 2.0 began in 2021. A further phase was agreed in 2023. Give local groups fair partnerships and support, not just more checks. Protect private data when publishing figures. Check the quality of the data and the funds local groups actually receive.
groups.source_review: Checked official IATI/UNHCR transparency commitments; Grand Bargain chronology and target retained as historical policy, not law. IASC direct retrieval/search was limited.
groups.notes: Corrected 2.0/2023 chronology and binding/real-time-tracking overclaims; target achievement not asserted.

groups.high: An exit strategy is a planned transition of responsibilities and resources, not simply a departure date. OECD work on transition financing emphasises coordinated, flexible support and avoiding financing gaps in fragile settings. Agencies should discuss likely changes early with affected people, local organisations, public authorities and other funders. Identify which essential services must continue, who will operate them, what skills and equipment are needed and how recurrent costs will be financed. Agree milestones, review dates and a realistic timetable for reducing or transferring support. Communicate limits and changes clearly. Monitor local capacity, unmet needs and security risks; revise the timetable when assumptions fail. Humanitarian and development needs can overlap, and recovery is not always linear. The end of an emergency phase does not automatically mean that all assistance should stop. The reviewed OECD guidance supports responsible transition planning, not a universal fixed withdrawal deadline for every agency or crisis.
groups.mid: An exit strategy plans a safe handover of services and resources. It is not simply a departure date. OECD work on transition finance calls for coordinated, flexible support that avoids funding gaps in fragile settings. Discuss likely changes early with affected communities, local organisations, public authorities and other funders. Identify essential services and who will run them. Check the skills, tools and ongoing funds they need. Agree milestones and review dates. Set a realistic timetable to reduce or transfer outside support. Explain limits and changes clearly so that people can plan. Monitor unmet needs, local capacity and security risks. Revise the timetable when the assumptions no longer hold. Recovery is not always a straight path from emergency to development. Both kinds of support may be needed at once. New conflict can reverse progress. The end of an emergency phase does not prove that all assistance should stop. The reviewed OECD guidance supports flexible transition planning. It sets no fixed withdrawal deadline for every agency or crisis.
groups.low: An exit plan is a safe handover, not just a date to leave. OECD guidance says support should be joined up and flexible so funds do not run out. Aid groups should discuss changes early with communities, local groups, public services and other funders. Decide what help must keep going and who will run it. Check the skills, tools and funds they will need, including day-to-day costs. Agree clear steps and dates to check before you cut or hand over support. Tell people what will change and what the limits are. Keep checking needs, local capacity and safety. Change the timetable if the plan no longer fits the facts. Recovery may go backwards as well as forwards. Emergency help and longer-term support may be needed at the same time. Do not treat the end of one project phase as proof that all help can stop. The OECD guidance does not set one fixed deadline for every agency to withdraw.
groups.source_review: Checked OECD flexible transition financing and coordination; no universal emergency-phase exit deadline found.
groups.notes: Qualified original claim that OECD requires withdrawal when emergency phase ends.
